Dear all,

I would much appreciate help to spread this add for a postdoc position in my group.

Sorry for cross-posting, thanks very much for your help.

Best regards,
Tord

Postdoc: Modelling future biodiversity, ecosystem services and climate

Depending on your expertise, you will develop models for the spatial distribution or dynamics of forest species, or make projections and optimizations using available models for biodiversity and ecosystem services assuming scenarios for the future. We answer ecological and conservation questions based om modelling distribution patterns or (meta)population dynamics of birds, beetles, plants, bryophytes, lichens and fungi. We further study how scenarios of socio-economic policy or development, climate change or forest management on different spatial scales (global, EU, landscape) may affect the future biodiversity, ecosystem services and climate. We also  investigate conflicts and synergies between these responses using a simulation & optimization framework. The work is funded by Formas and the ForestValue project  SustMultBiomass <https://www.researchgate.net/project/SustMultBiomass-Sustainable-and-multifunctional-use-of-forest-biomass>.

messages.subject: AW: CMR model with survival constrained by age (and environmental covariates)
messages.subject_clean: AW: CMR model with survival constrained by age (and environmental covariates)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarah,

To be able to use a different covariate for each age class, you can construct a matrix with your covariates, where the columns refer to years and the rows to the covariates. Row 1 may then be the particular covariate for age 1, row 2 that of age 2, aso. Assuming that your matrix is named X, you would then use the following line of code in your model:

       logit(phi[i,t]) <- alpha[age[i,t]] + eps[age[i,t],t] + beta[age[i,t]] * X[age[i,t],t]

Best wishes

Michael

Von: hmec...@googlegroups.com <hmec...@googlegroups.com> Im Auftrag von Sarah Durham
Gesendet: Dienstag, 7. März 2023 16:38
An: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology <hmec...@googlegroups.com>
Betreff: CMR model with survival constrained by age (and environmental covariates)

Hello everyone,

I have what I think is more of a coding question, but it's something I've been banging my head against a wall about for awhile now so I thought I'd just ask. I'm following example 7.7 in "Bayesian population analysis using WinBUGS" along with the example in the recent " Zero-inflated count distributions for capture–mark– reencounter data" from Riecke et al. (2022).

I am currently trying to figure out how I can constrain survival differently for juveniles and adults. I'm currently using an age matrix with nested indexing to account for the age structure, but I feel like this is causing problems when trying to incorporate different environemtnal covariates for the different age groups (but appears necessary for the curent CMR model structure). Currently I have the model set up to include random temporal effects,  but I'd like to eventually be able to include different environmental covariates for the different age groups (with juveniles being ages 0-3 and adults being aged 4+). I'm using only known-aged individuals in which exact age at marking is know. Any thoughts or suggestions about how to accomplish this would be grealty appreciated. I have the feeling it's an easy fix, I just can't seem to find to solution. Below I have pasted the pertinent parts of my code, happy to share some data if that would be helpful too. Cheers!

################ SELECTED CODE ################################

#Create age matrix covariate for known aged individuals
# Age 4 = average age of return, using this as break for juveniles/adults

# Juveniles ages 0-3, adults ages 4+

recode_ch <- function(ch, f){
  z <- ch
  for (i in 1:nrow(ch)) {
    for (j in 1:ncol(ch)) {
      if (j < (f[i])){z[i,j] <- NA}
      if (j == (f[i])){z[i,j] <- 1}
      if (j == (f[i]+1)){z[i,j] <- 1}
      if (j == (f[i]+2)){z[i,j] <- 1}
      if (j >= (f[i]+3)){z[i,j] <- 1}
      if (j >= (f[i]+4)){z[i,j] <- 2}
    }
  }
  z <- as.matrix(z)
  return(z)
}
age = recode_ch(j_ch,f.j)

###############################################################
CMR CODE
###############################################################

# Write JAGS model file
cat(file="ATPU_ZIGP.txt", "
model {
# Priors and constraints
for (i in 1:nind){
   for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
      logit(phi[i,t]) <- alpha[age[i,t]] + eps[age[i,t],t] # Constrain survival to be age-specific
      } #t
   } #i

for (u in 1:2){
   alpha[u] ~ dunif(0, 10)       # Priors for age and time specific survival
   }

for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
for (u in 1:2){
  eps[u,t] ~ dnorm(0,tau)
  }
}

# More priors

  epsilon ~ dgamma(1,1) # Prior for mean expected # encounters per individual
  gamma[1] ~ dbeta(1, 1)  # Prior for probability of availablity at time t given absense at time t-1
  gamma[2] ~ dbeta(1, 1) # Prior for probability of availablity at time t given available at time t-1
  sigma ~ dunif(0.5, 100)
  tau <- pow(sigma, -2)

 # Take inverse logit to backtransform survival probabilities
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
     phi.j[t] <- 1 / (1+exp(-alpha[1]-eps[1,t]))
     phi.a[t] <- 1 / (1+exp(-alpha[2]-eps[2,t]))
   }

###############################################################
CJS model
###############################################################
# Capture-recapture data (CJS model with multinomial likelihood)
# Define the multinomial likelihood

# CMR Model Likelihood components
for (i in 1:nind){

   for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

      z[i,t] ~ dbern(phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1])

      # State process
      a[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])
      mu1[i,t] <- z[i,t] * gamma[a[i,t-1]+1]

      # Observation process
      c[i,t] ~ dpois(mu2[i,t])
      mu2[i,t] <- a[i,t] * epsilon
      } #t
   } #i

} # end model

")

# Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("alpha","gamma","phi.j","phi.a", "epsilon")

inits <- function(){list(alpha = runif(2, 0, 1),
                         sigma = runif(1, 0.1, 10))}

ATPU_ZIGP_data <- list(z = z.dat,
                       a = a.dat,
                       f = f,
                       nind = dim(ch)[1],
                       n.occasions = dim(ch)[2],
                       c=c,
                       age=age)

# MCMC settings
ni <- 500000; nb <- 100000; nc <- 3; nt <- 3; na <- 5000

# Call JAGS
ATPU_ZIGP_out <- jags(ATPU_ZIGP_data, inits=inits, parameters, "ATPU_ZIGP.txt", n.iter=ni, n.burnin=nb, n.chains=nc, n.thin=nt, n.adapt=na, parallel = TRUE)

####################### END CODE ################################

--
*** Three hierarchical modeling email lists ***
(1) unmarked: for questions specific to the R package unmarked
(2) SCR: for design and Bayesian or non-bayesian analysis of spatial capture-recapture
(3) HMecology (this list): for everything else, especially material covered in the books by Royle & Dorazio (2008), Kéry & Schaub (2012), Kéry & Royle (2016, 2021) and Schaub & Kéry (2022)

messages.subject: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
messages.subject_clean: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I am trying to estimate weekly survival probabilities for young shorebirds over 6 occasions ranging from the last week of incubation to the fifth week of life after hatching using information from live encounters and dead recoveries. I am trying a slightly different approach than the Burnham model outlined in the BPA book, but similar idea.

I have formatted encounter histories using an age-based time structure – rather than a calendar-based time structure – to focus on the processes shaping survival of young from hatching to fledging. Occasions are defined in 7 d increments relative to the hatch date of each individual. All individuals enter the analysis on occasion 1, as eggs in their last week of incubation. Subsequent encounters with individual young are detailed for occasions 2 to 6, the first to fifth weeks of life after hatching.

Three states are defined in the model: 1) alive, 2) recently dead, and 3) dead (absorbing). There are three types of encounters: 1) live detections, 2) dead recoveries, and 3) non-detections.

I am getting hung up on a couple of things. In addition to being interested in several fixed effects (including hatch date), I am exploring two different random effects on survival, detection, and recovery parameters: siteyear effects and brood effects. There are many models to consider that seem like reasonable hypotheses.

Nimble appears to generate WAIC values fine but in some cases a "better" model according to WAIC shows poor mixing of chains for some parameters. Should I be prioritizing WAIC or mixing of chains and convergence of estimates? Or should I be thinking about different parameterizations? Or a totally different way to model these data? Or...?

Many thanks,

Justin

Attached is some test code which may or may not be helpful.

messages.subject: Open post-doc position in Sempach
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

We are looking for a post-doctoral researcher to enhance our team at the Population Biology unit at the Vogelwarte in Sempach. Details can be found on the attachment and below. Please feel free to spread the announcement.

Thank you!

Best wishes

Michael

The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach is a non-profit foundation supported by the public

and focuses on a wide range of research topics on wild birds within and beyond Switzerland.

We aim at acquiring the scientific basis for a deeper understanding of biological systems

and for the conservation of birds and their habitats.

The population biology research group is currently a team of five persons that aims to study

population dynamics of birds and to develop or adjust the needed statistical methodology.

We are looking for a

Post-doctoral researcher in population ecology

(m/f/d), 100%

to enhance the team in the unit Population Biology from the  1st of September 2023 or by

agreement.

You will analyze long-term demographic data (capture-recapture, productivity, population

counts) of dippers and alpine swifts in Switzerland using integrated population models to better

understand the population dynamics of these species. The dipper data set is from a single

study area, while the swift data are from multiple breeding colonies. Particular focus will be on

understanding demographic drivers (including immigration) of the observed population changes

and on population synchrony.

We expect a completed PhD in ecology, wildlife science or a related field. A deep understanding

of population models (including capture-recapture, matrix population models), hierarchical

models, computation (e.g., R or Python), and Bayesian modeling software (e.g., JAGS, NIMBLE

or STAN) is required, as is a proven desire and ability to publish excellent papers.

What we offer

The position is initially limited to 2 years with the option of an extension. You interact with a

variety of people while you also have flexibility to plan your work. Salary is according to the

regulation of the Swiss Ornithological Institute and incudes social benefits. In addition, you can

expect family-friendly and flexible working hours, good opportunities for further training and

exemplary social benefits. The place of work is Sempach.

You are interested?

The Swiss Ornithological Institute is committed to promoting diversity and looks forward to

receiving applications from as many qualified individuals as possible. For more details on the

position, please contact Michael Schaub, Head of unit Population Biology.

We look forward to receiving your online application by latest 30th April 2023. Please upload

your application documents (cover letter with statement of motivation, CV, copies of diplomas)

in a single PDF file to https://my.jobalino.ch/de/jobpreview/4563.

Job interviews for invited applicants are planned for the 15th and 16th May 2023.

Michael Schaub
Leiter Bereich "Populationsbiologie"
Dozent an der Universität Bern

messages.subject_clean: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Justin,

I'll take a shot. Note, just one person's opinion.
If I were trying to select a model that has the best (leave-one-out) cross-validation properties, I might use WAIC. If interested in coverage of the 95% CI's (and not too worried about prediction uncertainty), I might just fit one "full model" with all of the pre-specified effects.
If a model was not converging or mixing well, I wouldn't trust/report the WAIC score. It's possible that nimble is throwing warnings about point-wise pWAIC>0.4 or whatever--if so, I would similarly not trust the score. Tactically, if a more complex model were scoring much better and the posterior indicates support for the random effects or whatever other added bells/whistles (e.g., sd's >>0) , I might focus on tinkering around to help convergence/mixing of this model. This might include swapping samplers, blocking certain terms, marginalizing over the the discrete latent states (e.g., nimbleEcology's dHMM family of distributions), etc. Tough to say what to do here. I might also check priors/employ a prior predictive check to make sure certain things are sensible. Just as an example, inv.logit(N(0, sd=5)) is bimodal, which may or may not be reasonable; the exponential distribution has a long-right tail, and something like a half normal might be better behaved.
Where this gets tricky is in the WAIC calculations, where there is some hand-wringing about conditioning on vs. marginalizing over random effects and where default calculations may not be what you want. Random effects here include the varied sds, and also the z's. I think nimbleMCMC uses the fully conditional WAIC. I think this implies that the score/penalty parts of the IC are derived from log([y_{i,t}|z_{i,t}*po_{i,t}]), which is a little like scoring the model based on how well the detection model (alone) fits. Using dHMM to marginalize over z, the model will be scored using log([y_{i,}|ps_{i,},po_{i, ]), which includes the contributions of the state model to the data likelihood. I think others are working on alternative approaches that would also capture the contributions of the state model.
With the brood and site-year random effects, nimble provides some ways to control whether you want to marginalize over these effects and how you want to group data if you do. These are dense topics, and the links below and related are better references--it seems this has some connection to whether the comparison is predicated on leaving one individual out vs. leaving one brood or site-year out.

https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-017-9736-8
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31297664/
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.13359.pdf

John

messages.subject_clean: Live encounters and dead recoveries and model selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

Thank you for offering your thoughts and links to references. I will confess that I am not excited to hear that some of the references cover "dense topics"!

A couple of notes that may be of general interest: I did try using a couple of different distributions for the standard deviations of the random brood effects. Constraining those SDs with a uniform distribution dunif(0,3) did enable better convergence of parameter estimates...but I'm pretty sure it also resulted in underestimates of the true heterogeneity of survival and detection processes. Some broods probably are much more likely to survive than others. Some broods probably are much more likely to be detected than others. So, I suspect the long-tailed exponential distribution is warranted, at least in theory. As a potential alternative to modeling random brood effects, I have also tinkered with analyzing bootstraps of data (encounter histories for one individual from each brood). I do not think this is a great solution in this system.

I am going to try a few more things and push ahead.

Thanks again.

Justin
